notes.meaning: Eliphaz speaks up again to begin the second round of speeches. He is upset that Job refused the advice given earlier and dared to challenge God. Instead of feeling sympathy, Eliphaz prepares a sharper attack against his friend.

Eliphaz asks whether a truly wise person would answer with windy, useless words. In that region, the hot east wind from the desert was fierce and destructive. Eliphaz claims that Job's speeches are full of harmful, empty air rather than true wisdom.

Eliphaz argues that a wise man should not waste time with worthless talk. He claims Job's arguments have no solid weight and help nobody. Our words should always aim to build others up rather than vent frustration.

Eliphaz accuses Job of tearing down reverence for God and hindering prayer. He assumes that if Job claims God lets the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper, people will see no point in praying. He mistakenly believes Job's honest cries will lead others into unbelief.

Eliphaz claims that Job's sinful heart is directing what he says. He accuses Job of using sneaky, crafty words to hide his lack of respect for God, like the serpent in Eden. In Eliphaz's eyes, clever speech cannot cover up hidden guilt.

Eliphaz tells Job that his own words serve as the ultimate witness against him. He claims he does not even need to judge Job, because Job's complaints already condemn him. It is easy for an unkind listener to twist an honest cry of grief into proof of wrongdoing.

Eliphaz asks mockingly if Job was the very first human being ever created. He asks whether Job existed before the hills were shaped, acting as if he owned the original wisdom of creation. He uses these biting questions to bring down Job's confidence.

Eliphaz asks whether Job sat in on God's secret heavenly council to learn all His plans. He wonders if Job thinks he has cornered the market on wisdom. He throws Job's earlier sarcastic remarks right back at him.

Eliphaz asks what Job understands that the three friends do not already know. He refuses to admit that Job has any deeper spiritual insight than they do. He believes their shared knowledge is more than enough to explain Job's troubles.

Eliphaz points to the aged, gray-haired elders on his side, noting that some are older than Job's own father. In the ancient world, old age was deeply honored as the source of true insight. Eliphaz leans on long life experience to prove that his view must be right.

Eliphaz asks if the comforts God offers through the friends' gentle advice are not good enough for Job. He treats his own speeches as if they were God's own consolation. He takes it as personal pride that Job refuses to accept their words.

Eliphaz asks why Job lets his emotions sweep him away and why his eyes flash with anger. He thinks Job is acting proud, stubborn, and scornful toward his comforters. He views Job's deep pain merely as an uncontrolled temper.

Eliphaz accuses Job of aiming his spirit in anger directly against God and spouting reckless complaints. He sees Job's bold questions as open rebellion against the Almighty. He fails to see that a hurting believer can pour out confusion to God without hating Him.

Eliphaz repeats the idea that no human being born into this world can ever be perfectly pure or righteous before God. He uses Job's own phrase about being born of a woman to remind him of human weakness. He argues that Job has no right to claim he is innocent.

Eliphaz reminds Job that God does not even place complete trust in His holy angels, and even the heavens are not pure in His sight. Compared to the perfect holiness of the Creator, even heavenly creatures have limits. Nothing created can match God's absolute purity.

Eliphaz says human beings are far less pure, being naturally corrupt and gulping down sin like water. He means that people run after wrongdoing as easily and greedily as a thirsty traveler drinks in the desert. He aims this hard truth directly at Job to show he is a sinner in need of repentance.

Eliphaz asks Job to listen closely while he explains what he has personally witnessed. He sets out to prove his claim that severe misery falls only on the wicked. He bases his teaching on both personal observation and time-tested facts.

Eliphaz explains that his conclusions come from ancient sages who received them faithfully from their fathers. These wise men did not hide the truth but passed it down carefully from generation to generation. He believes this unbroken chain of teaching cannot be wrong.

Eliphaz notes that these ancient fathers held the land all to themselves without any foreign invaders mixing among them. Because their culture was pure and undisturbed, he believes their wisdom was kept clean from outside errors. He uses this ancient pure heritage to give weight to his words.

Eliphaz teaches that the wicked person lives in constant inner torment throughout his whole life. A cruel tyrant never knows how many years he has left before judgment falls. He argues that behind any show of outward success, an oppressor is always full of secret dread.

Eliphaz says frightening sounds constantly haunt the ears of the wicked, filling them with alarm. Even in peaceful and prosperous days, a guilty conscience makes them fear that an attacker will suddenly strike. A life of sin robs a person of true inner peace.

Eliphaz says the wicked man despairs of ever escaping from dark trouble and expects to be killed by the sword. His guilty mind makes him see danger lurking in every shadow. Eliphaz hints that Job's despair over his condition shows he shares the mindset of the ungodly.

Eliphaz describes the wicked man wandering desperately for food, knowing that utter ruin is near. Having once taken bread from others by force, he now faces starvation and total defeat. His guilty conscience warns him that his dark end has already arrived.

Eliphaz says distress and sharp anguish crush the sinner like a mighty king charging into battle. The terrors within his soul are too powerful for him to fight off. Troubles overtake him completely because he has no shelter in God.

Eliphaz explains why this ruin happens: the wicked person shook his fist in defiance against God. He acted with proud arrogance against the Almighty, thinking he could stand on his own. Eliphaz views all unrepentant sin as a foolish battle declared against the Lord.

Eliphaz pictures the rebel soldier charging headlong at God with a stiff neck and a heavy, metal-studded shield. The sinner foolishly thinks his own strength and defenses can protect him from God's justice. It is total madness for a frail creature to rush against an almighty Maker.

Eliphaz points out that the rebel grew fat and heavy around the waist from pampering himself in luxury. His easy wealth made him proud, secure, and careless toward God and people. Physical plenty often tempts the human heart to forget its need for the Lord.

Eliphaz says the oppressor ends up living in desolate cities and crumbling houses destined to become piles of rubble. Even if a tyrant conquers towns or rebuilds ruins to make a great name for himself, God brings his efforts to nothing. Human power cannot turn God's curse into a lasting home.

Eliphaz states that the wicked person's wealth will dry up and will not spread across the land. Whatever he gained through violence or pride will slip away from his hands. God ensures that dishonest gain never produces lasting security.

Eliphaz says the wicked cannot escape from darkness, for God's fiery judgment will wither their branches and His breath will blow them away. He compares the oppressor's family and wealth to green shoots dried up by scorching heat. With a single word or breath, God easily wipes out His enemies.

Eliphaz warns that anyone who deceives himself by trusting in empty things will receive only emptiness as his reward. Chasing after false security or wealth leaves a person with nothing of real value. Placing our confidence in anything less than God will always disappoint us.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary agrees that vanity is the sinner's reward, but adds that the person could still find safety if they turned back to God in true repentance.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz says the sinner's life and prosperity will be cut short before his full time, like a branch that loses its greenness. He will not live out a peaceful old age, and his household will fade away. Sin brings an untimely end to hopes that once looked bright.

Eliphaz compares the wicked person to a grapevine that drops its grapes before they ripen, or an olive tree that sheds its flowers. His plans and his children will fail to reach full maturity. His life ends up fruitless because it was rooted in selfishness.

Eliphaz declares that the families of godless people will end up childless and barren, and fire will consume the homes of those who take bribes. This was a stinging hint aimed at Job, whose children and houses were destroyed by sudden disaster and fire. Eliphaz wrongly presumes that Job's losses came from secret dishonesty.

Eliphaz finishes by saying that the wicked conceive trouble in their minds and give birth only to evil and deceit. They spend their energy plotting harm against others, but their schemes end up fooling and ruining themselves. Sin always turns back on the one who plans it.
